title.text: Tayabas Basilica of St. Michael the Archangel

title_en.text: Basilica Minore of St. Michael the Archangel

tagline.text: A Spanish-era church known for its key-shaped plan and 103 m nave

location.label: Location
location.text: Central Tayabas, Quezon (St. Michael the Archangel Basilica, near the city hall)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (excluding the September 29 feast day)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱600–1,500 (day trip from Manila, including transport and meals; rough estimate)

children.text: The Basilica of St. Michael the Archangel stands in the center of Tayabas, Quezon. Its origins go back to the 16th century, it was raised to a minor basilica in 1988, and it was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001. Its key-shaped cruciform plan, nave of about 103 m, and old monumental clock tower are its main sights.

The Basilica Minore of St. Michael the Archangel is a Roman Catholic church in the heart of Tayabas, Quezon. Its official name is the Minor Basilica of St. Michael the Archangel and Diocesan Shrine of San Diego de Alcalá, and it belongs to the Diocese of Lucena. Locals call it Susì ng Tayabas, meaning "the Key of Tayabas," because its floor plan looks like a key when seen from above. It lies roughly 150 km south of Manila, so it is an easy day trip from the capital.

The church's roots go back to the early Spanish colonial period. According to the records, Franciscan friars brought the Catholic faith to Tayabas in 1578, and in 1585 Tayabas became a parish with St. Michael as its patron saint. The first church was a modest building of bamboo, nipa and anahaw leaves; around 1590 permission was obtained to build in stone, and in 1600 it was rebuilt in brick. An earthquake in 1743 left only the walls standing, and it was rebuilt afterward. It has been repaired many times since: between 1856 and 1866, under Fr. Benito de la Pila, the round transept and dome were added, and in 1894 the brick-tile roof was replaced with galvanized iron. During World War II the convent was reportedly used as a Japanese garrison. A rededication Mass was held on March 14, 1987, and a major renovation in 2000 moved the altar to the crossing beneath the dome. In 2011, about 1,798 m² of roof and framework were repaired together with the National Museum. Thanks to this history, the church is regarded not as a mere old building but as living heritage that the townspeople have protected for generations.

The building is classed as Baroque, though the interior has a strongly Neoclassical feel, with seven altars. Its most remarkable feature is its length. The nave (central aisle) measures about 103 m and is counted among the longest of any Spanish colonial-era church. Pope John Paul II raised it to a minor basilica in 1988, and in 2001 the National Museum named it one of 26 Philippine churches declared National Cultural Treasures. It has also reportedly been declared a diocesan shrine honoring San Diego de Alcalá, so check locally for the latest news.

Tayabas tourism calls the minor basilica’s key-shaped plan Susi ng Tayabas, or “Key of Tayabas.” In June 2026 the city discussed repairs with national cultural and historical agencies. On days with services or works, ask the
Tayabas tourism office
or parish which areas are accessible.
The church has a cruciform plan, so from above it looks like a key. Walking the nave of about
from the entrance to the altar gives you a real sense of its scale.

The façade has three tiers, and statues of the archangels Michael, Gabriel and Raphael stand on the top level. Look closely at the decoration, which mixes several styles, including niches and capiz-shell windows.
Stone lions at the entrance are explained as a sign of pre-colonial trade links with China. You can also find stone cherubs playing musical instruments.

A dome rises above the round transept added in the 19th century, and the main altar enshrines Our Lady of the Angels (Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles). The ceiling painting is said to have been restored in the 1990s.

The bell tower holds a large clock said to have been installed in the early 20th century, and it chimes on the hour and half hour. It is described as one of the oldest and largest church clocks in Asia.
The façade lighting was reportedly converted to solar power in 2011. The church at dusk, with its lights on, also makes a good photo.

blocks.title: Ermita chapels and the old cemetery

children.text: Around the church are small chapels (ermitas) dedicated to Our Lady of Sorrows and San Diego de Alcalá, and an old stone cemetery chapel with two towers also survives. Check locally whether they are open.

There is a record that on August 13, 1898, the troops of General Vicente Lukban received the surrender of the Spanish forces on this church's patio. Keep in mind that a scene from the Philippine Revolution took place here as you walk around.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The church's architecture and downtown Tayabas

children.text: Leave Manila on a bus to Lucena. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so leave some margin.
Transfer in Lucena to a jeepney or van bound for Tayabas. Get off in downtown Tayabas and walk toward the church.
Start with the exterior and façade. Look in turn at the three tiers, the statues, the stone lions and the clock on the bell tower.
When no Mass is under way, go inside to see the long nave, the dome, the altar and the ceiling painting. If worshippers are praying, move quietly.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town. You could also look for Lucban's pancit habhab or other local dishes nearby.
If you have time, stroll through Tayabas to see old buildings and the patio, and check your return transport in good time.
Masses and services take priority inside the church. Plan your visit to avoid Mass times.
Leave Manila early, arrive in Lucena, and continue to Tayabas.
Visit the Basilica of St. Michael the Archangel in Tayabas.
Have lunch in Tayabas or Lucban. Lucban is known for its pancit habhab.
Move on to Lucban and look around its town center and church. Lucban is in the same province and is linked by jeepney.
Return to Lucena and take a bus back to Manila. Check the time of the last bus in advance.
On May 15, the day of the Pahiyas Festival, Lucban is extremely crowded, so allow plenty of travel time.
A listed JAC Liner example from Kamias in the Cubao area to Lucena Grand Central Terminal is
one way. Trips from Buendia or PITX have separate fares and options, so check your terminal.
The
Lucena terminal directory
lists the Jollibee by the Lucena–Tayabas Road junction as a boarding point for Tayabas jeepneys. Ask the driver where to get off for the basilica.
Another Cubao listing shows a one-way fare of
. Check the Kamias pickup point, final ticket price and travel time before booking.
Tayabas is a neighboring city of Lucena, so using Lucena as your base is convenient.
From Manila, take the South Luzon Expressway toward Quezon province. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so leave some margin.
Parking near the church may be limited, so check locally where the town parking lots are.
Tricycles are a common way to get around Tayabas. Fares depend on distance and bargaining, so confirm before you ride.
The area around the church can be explored on foot.

Tayabas is best visited from December to May, when rainfall is relatively low. To explore the church inside and out on foot, early morning or late afternoon is less hot. May is the hottest season in the Philippines, so around midday it is best to rest in the shade inside the church.

If you want to see the events, plan your dates accordingly. The feast of St. Michael is September 29, and during Holy Week a passion play and processions take place on the church patio. During events the crowds make it hard to see the interior in peace. Programs can change from year to year, so check the parish announcements before you go.

If you only want to see the church, a day trip from Manila is possible, but if you also want to add the Pahiyas Festival in Lucban, it is more comfortable to spend a night in Lucena. Lucena is Quezon's transport hub with the most hotels and restaurants, and Tayabas itself has a few small lodgings, so check local information before booking.

Look for Quezon's signature dishes. Lucban's pancit habhab is a dry stir-fried noodle dish often sold on banana leaves, and Lucban longganisa sausage is also famous. Tayabas and Lucban are close, so you can try the food of both. Local sweets and souvenirs can be found in shops in town, and prices should be checked locally.
The church is still a place of worship, so modest dress covering shoulders and knees is recommended. Take off your hat inside.
During Mass, refrain from taking photos and making noise, and walk around from places where you will not disturb worshippers' prayers.
The nave is long, so a wide-angle lens or your phone's wide-angle mode helps for photos.
The bell-tower clock chimes on the hour and half hour, so if you time your visit you can hear it too.
It is hot at midday, so bring water, a hat and sunscreen. The inside of the church is relatively cool.
Many places need cash, so carry small bills. Check where the ATMs in town are beforehand.
During events such as the Pahiyas Festival in Lucban or the feast of St. Michael, lodging and transport fill up early.
Confirm individual worship and visiting hours with the parish. For a group visiting Casa Comunidad as well, use
Tayabas City’s tour assistance
to arrange your date, group size and route.
The area around the church has old houses and shops in a row, so walk slowly between the buildings and enjoy the old atmosphere of Tayabas.
The feast of Our Lady of Sorrows just before Holy Week (Viernes Dolores de Turumba) is said to feature dancing, chanting and a procession, so if your dates match, check local announcements.
The church is an active place of worship. Move quietly so as not to disturb Mass and services, and follow the photography rules.
On event days, beware of pickpockets and crowds, and carry your bag in front of you.
The opening hours and whether interior photography is allowed may vary depending on the parish.
The nave floor is old stone and can be slippery, so avoid high heels.
If there is a typhoon or rain, the trip between Lucena and Tayabas can take longer.
If anyone pressures you for donations, politely decline and use only the official donation box.
A guide to the city where the church stands. You can see the Mayohan festival and old buildings downtown together.
A nearby neighboring town known for pancit habhab and longganisa.
A transport hub for travelers from Manila and a good place to find lodging.
A harvest thanksgiving festival held in Lucban every May 15, easy to combine with a May itinerary.
